stories.headline: Trump's Iran remarks on LA and San Diego draw backlash, White House defends

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: Trump made remarks at a campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska on Monday.
Trump said while discussing the Iran conflict: 'They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego... This is a very small price to pay.'
California Gov. Gavin Newsom called the comments 'deranged and dangerous'.
Newsom later said Trump is 'mentally ill'.
Newsom called for invocation of the 25th Amendment.
LA Mayor Karen Bass said the remarks were a threat meant to 'encourage attacks on American lives'.
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said the city was not 'collateral damage' and demanded Trump keep it out of his 'reckless war talk'.
White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said Trump was stating that U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped by his administration's war.
The official White House Rapid Response account said Trump was stating that U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped by his administration's war.
Newsom directed California's State Threat Assessment Center to monitor for the possibility that foreign actors interpret Trump's remarks as an invitation to target the state.
San Diego hosts Naval Base San Diego (home port of the Pacific Fleet), Naval Amphibious Base Coronado, and Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton (70,000 service members and civilians).
Los Angeles hosts the Space Force's space systems command headquarters and Los Angeles Air Force Base.
CNN fact-checker Daniel Dale said he read Trump's 'small price to pay' comment as referring to war costs like gas prices, not to Iran attacking the cities.
Senior reporter Aaron Blake said he read Trump's 'small price to pay' comment as referring to war costs like gas prices, not to Iran attacking the cities.
Former Trump staffer Sarah Matthews said she read Trump's 'small price to pay' comment as referring to war costs like gas prices, not to Iran attacking the cities.
Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer condemned the remarks.
Sen. Chris Murphy condemned the remarks.
California gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra said the cities' 13 million residents are not a 'small price to pay'.

The controversy stems from ambiguous phrasing in a campaign speech about the U.S.-Iran conflict, where Trump invoked Los Angeles and San Diego — both home to major military installations — while arguing that the costs of the war were justified.
The dispute centers on whether his words implied Iran should be allowed to strike the cities, or whether he meant those cities would have faced a nuclear threat from Iran had the U.S. not acted.
This is the latest flashpoint in a long-running feud between Trump and Newsom.
Newsom has publicly sparred with the president over immigration enforcement, military deployments to California, and personal remarks about Newsom's dyslexia.
Newsom is viewed as a potential 2028 presidential contender.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom called the remarks 'deranged and dangerous' and later said Trump is 'mentally ill,' urging 25th Amendment removal.
LA Mayor Karen Bass said the comments constituted a threat intended to 'encourage attacks on American lives'.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer condemned the remarks as 'deranged,' 'delusional,' and 'sick,' calling the cities' residents 'collateral damage'.
Sen. Chris Murphy condemned the remarks as 'deranged,' 'delusional,' and 'sick,' calling the cities' residents 'collateral damage'.

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said critics' characterization was 'not rooted in reality' and that Trump meant U.S. cities would have been threatened by a nuclear Iran had it not been stopped.
The official White House Rapid Response account said Trump was describing the U.S. fighting to prevent Iran from having the ability to strike LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon.

The core disagreement is a matter of interpretation rather than an outright factual dispute: both readings of Trump's ambiguous phrasing — that the 'small price to pay' refers to war costs versus to Iran's hypothetical attack on the cities — are plausible from the same quote.
Even some of Trump's frequent critics declined to embrace the harshest interpretation.
The exchange is likely to deepen the ongoing political rift between Trump and Newsom ahead of the 2026 midterms and potential 2028 presidential positioning.
The exchange is likely to heighten scrutiny of how national-security rhetoric from elected officials is parsed and amplified by media and rapid-response accounts on both sides.

stories.headline: France suspends stun grenades after boy loses hand in student protest
body: France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests after a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a demonstration in Lens on Monday. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of the incident had been "clarified," as conflicting accounts emerged from protesters and officials. The boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade—a weapon considered non-lethal that releases small rubber pellets upon detonation—was fired near the Auguste Béhal high school. Authorities said the boy picked up the grenade before it exploded, while students alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired. According to the local prefect, police had been confronted by more than 200 students throwing stones and fireworks.

The protests, which began among high school pupils and have since spread to parents, university students, and unions, continued Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be closed for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils. On Tuesday, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to call for better school conditions; the interior ministry reported 488 arrests and 43 security force members injured. Officials said more than 200 students and 700 police officers have been harmed overall, with more than 6,500 arrests since the unrest began.

Nuñez told French radio RTL that the police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations. "There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said. The national secretary of policing union UNSA, Jean-Paul Nascimento, expressed skepticism about the suspension, saying it was based "on emotion" and warning that without the weapon to disperse crowds, "there will perhaps be even more injuries."

Concerns about police tactics have been stoked by other incidents. A 14-year-old was hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, northwest of Paris, losing several teeth and suffering a fractured jaw; a police officer has been charged. On Wednesday, a 16-year-old suffered a serious hand injury outside a school in Strasbourg while reportedly handling a mortar firework. In Belfort, prosecutors opened an investigation for attempted murder after a 17-year-old protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river; the boy has himself been charged with aggravated assault for allegedly attacking the officer.

Addressing the National Assembly on Wednesday, Nuñez and Geffray said the speed at which the protests turned violent was unprecedented. Geffray alleged the movement had been "very quickly infiltrated by ultra-violent groups" and said dozens of headteachers and deputies had been injured, many deliberately. Nuñez later said he found it "excessive to speak of police repression of the movement," insisting officers acted only in response to violence and damage. The national coordinator of the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party said it had taken "several children being maimed for life for Nuñez to give up using grenades against high school students." Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has accused LFI of trying to "sow chaos" ahead of April elections to choose President Emmanuel Macron's successor.

President Macron held an emergency meeting late Tuesday with Lecornu and other key ministers. Lecornu announced that schools should set aside half the day for students to voice their concerns and noted that an online consultation had drawn 30,000 responses within a day. Students' unions, who put the number of Tuesday's protesters at 450,000, said a fourth round of demonstrations is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities. The union representing school leaders told FranceInfo that a solution would require "something more than simple consultation periods," while the head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, said: "We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint."

stories.headline: Three years after 7 October attacks, Israelis demand accountability for security failures
body: Three years after the deadliest attack in Israel's history, survivors and families of those killed on 7 October 2023 are demanding a state inquiry into the security failures that allowed Hamas-led gunmen to kill about 1,200 people and take 251 hostages. In Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 kidnapped, Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed and four other relatives taken, said: 'I need my country to take responsibility.' Despite the scale of the assault, no independent state commission of inquiry has been established, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was in charge at the time, has rejected personal responsibility and is running for re-election on a security platform.

Questions are mounting over what Netanyahu knew before the attack. Reports have emerged of warnings from Israel's own security chief and regional neighbours, including an allegation published by Haaretz that the UAE leader called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans. Netanyahu's office dismissed the report as 'an absolute lie' and said he would sue the newspaper. Amir Ohana of Netanyahu's Likud party called the suggestion 'preposterous and absurd', arguing that even Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar had told only a handful of people. Netanyahu has blamed his security chiefs, saying they deliberately chose not to wake him in the hours beforehand for fear he would order a massive IDF deployment. 'God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, "Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!"' he told Channel 14. 'What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened.'

Journalist Yaacov Katz, author of 'While Israel Slept', said that in the early hours of 7 October, senior military and intelligence figures expected at worst a small incursion, making a pre-emptive strike unlikely. He argued that Netanyahu faced deeper questions about his policy of containing Hamas in Gaza, which allowed Qatar to send hundreds of millions of dollars in aid. Netanyahu has denied wanting to strengthen Hamas, telling Die Welt the money was 'meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe'. Katz said: 'You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state.'

Within the military, accountability has been accepted. The IDF's former chief of staff, Lt Gen Herzi Halevi, publicly apologised and resigned; a raft of commanders were fired; and Israel's domestic intelligence chief left his post. Col Richard Hecht, the IDF's international spokesman on 7 October, resigned six months later, citing the refusal of political leaders to accept responsibility. 'It's a disgrace,' he said. 'When you look at accountability, within the IDF I don't think there's a problem. And that's the pain. That's one of the main causes of bad blood between the political echelon and the military.' At a memorial ceremony in Jerusalem, the father of a victim stood up to challenge Netanyahu, saying, 'You didn't protect my son, you didn't protect all those who were murdered,' before being led away by security guards.

Campaigners have asked Israel's highest court to force the government to establish a state commission of inquiry. Yizhar Shai, a former minister whose son Yaron was killed on 7 October, said: 'We are going into these elections almost blindfolded as it relates to October 7th. Our prime minister has never given a detailed, thorough explanation under oath, where he would be asked all the tough questions and have to explain everything.' Netanyahu has refused a state inquiry led by the Supreme Court, arguing the judiciary would be biased. His government proposed an alternative 'national commission of inquiry' with members appointed by political parties, but ran out of time to pass the enabling bill before parliament ended its session in July. The denial of responsibility has become an election issue, with Netanyahu's opponent Gadi Eisenkot releasing a video game called 'Sleepy Bibi' that asks players to help the prime minister avoid warnings and 'make it to bed safely'.

Polls suggest a close race, with the 7 October attacks central to many voters' decisions. Katz described the legacy as a coin with two sides: 'There are the failures, the mistakes that led to the Hamas invasion. But there's the other side, which is Netanyahu's argument; that [he] has re-engineered the Middle East and made Israel a safer place today. And that is an argument Israelis take with them to the polls.' For supporters, Netanyahu remains the man to keep Israel safe; critics say his political survival puts the country at risk.

stories.headline: Trump says he will speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
body: US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia. "So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with the Russian leader "probably" on Thursday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled.

Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague. They insist there is no risk of an epidemic. Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death. The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier. Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after either breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.

Pneumonic plague is a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague. According to the WHO, it has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal if not diagnosed and treated early. People can be infected through infected flea bites, contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials, or the inhalation of respiratory particles. Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm. The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area. It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death. It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East was founded just over 100 years ago.

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for transparency from Russia. "Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice, and accused the media of reporting "false information". The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.

In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities". However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection. Rospotrebnadzor later said "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region", adding that more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected".

Neighbouring Mongolia's government has ordered "health surveillance" measures on its border with Russia, AFP news agency reported. The country's health ministry said it would "maintain continuous surveillance and monitoring to prevent potential risks", describing it as a precautionary measure and adding "the current risk level is low." Lithuania's health ministry said it has made preparations to manage any possible case in the country. Laboratory testing is available, patients would be isolated in infectious disease hospitals, contacts would be identified, and the country has stocks of medicines suitable for treatment, according to Nerija Kaulakien, an adviser at the Ministry of Health's Communications Division, in an interview with ELTA news agency. There was no evidence of "an increased risk of plague" at the moment, she said.

Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.

stories.headline: Zelensky condemns 'vile' large-scale Russian attacks that killed at least 24 across Ukraine
body: At least 24 people were killed and dozens more wounded in a wave of Russian missile strikes across central and eastern Ukraine overnight, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday, calling it one of Moscow's 'most vile' attacks. Zelensky said 70 missiles were launched in total, hitting cities including Kyiv, Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Zaporizhzhia, Oleksandriya, and Pryluky in the Chernihiv region, where a five-story residential building was destroyed. He described the strike on Pryluky as a 'birthday gift' to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who turns 74 on Wednesday.

The heaviest toll was in Pryluky, where Zelensky said 18 people, including four children, were killed. Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported 50 people injured in that attack, including seven children. Two people were killed in Kyiv and two others in Oleksandriya, Zelensky added. Ukraine's national police released verified images of an unexploded Russian Iskander missile in a Kyiv district, and video showed rescuers digging through collapsed rubble in Pryluky.

Zelensky said one of the 'key targets' of the assault was Ukraine's energy infrastructure, following Moscow's earlier pledge to intensify such strikes in retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities. He renewed a call for allies to provide more air defense support, noting that Ukraine's military managed to shoot down only 'some' of the incoming missiles.

In the same 24-hour period, Zelensky said Ukraine struck four targets in retaliatory attacks on Russia's Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions, including two oil facilities and a training ground. 'There is also a response in the Black Sea,' he wrote, without providing details. On Tuesday evening, footage showed a large plume of smoke from an oil tanker off the coast of Sochi, Russia. The Russian transport ministry said unmanned boats had attacked the Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio tanker, and that the crew was rescued.

Separately, Bulgaria suspended a search for the missing crew of a civilian cargo ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday in the Black Sea, according to Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov of Bulgaria's Maritime Administration. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said a second vessel carrying grain was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, but its 18 crew members were rescued. Bulgaria has not attributed the attacks to any party. Moscow has not commented on the latest incidents involving the Black Sea shipping, though Zelensky accused Russia of being responsible for those attacks as well.

Zelensky's condemnation and plea for air defense underscore the ongoing urgency for Western support as Ukraine continues to face large-scale missile barrages while carrying out its own cross-border operations.

stories.headline: Sri Lanka's ex-first lady arrested over alleged misuse of children's hospital donations
body: Sri Lanka's former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been arrested on allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations raised for a children's hospital. The 73-year-old wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa was taken into custody by anti-corruption authorities at their Colombo home on Wednesday.

Authorities are questioning her over 10 million rupees ($30,300; £22,800) in donations collected by the Siriliya Saviya charity, intended for a specialised scanner at Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital. Officials say such a scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government.

Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing and says the money has not been appropriated. She returned to Sri Lanka on Monday from Singapore, where she was receiving medical treatment. She had filed a court petition to try to prevent her arrest, but the hearing was set for 12 October.

Ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa's spokesperson, Manoj Gamage, has said the money is safe in Siriliya's accounts and that no fraud has occurred. Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president from 2005 to 2015, and his family held a tight grip over the country's politics for years. He was hailed by many as a hero for ending nearly three decades of civil war when Tamil Tiger rebels were crushed in 2009.

In 2022, protests broke out across Sri Lanka as inflation surged and the country ran out of fuel, food and medicine. Mahinda's brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was serving as leader at that time, was eventually toppled. Sri Lanka's current government, under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has since revived long-stalled corruption investigations involving various members of the Rajapaksa family.

Mahinda and Shiranthi's eldest son, Namal Rajapaksa, was arrested earlier this year over allegations linked to an aircraft procurement deal made during his father's presidency and is currently held in remand. His brother Yoshitha was also arrested earlier this year on corruption charges.

stories.headline: Stocks Slide as Treasury Yields Hit 24-Year High; Fed Minutes Awaited
body: U.S. stocks fell sharply on Wednesday, retreating from record highs as Treasury yields surged to their highest levels in more than two decades. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped roughly 500 points, or about 1.1%, while the S&P 500 declined 0.6% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.7%. The pullback came a day after the S&P 500 closed above 7,800 for the first time and the Nasdaq hit an all-time high, driven by bullish earnings estimates and gains in major technology stocks.

The sell-off was led by a renewed spike in bond yields. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield climbed more than 8 basis points to trade at 5.356%, its highest level since April 2002. The 30-year bond yield rose a similar amount to 5.725%, the highest since May 2002. The moves came ahead of a Treasury auction of $39 billion in 10-year notes and as investors awaited the release of minutes from the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting, when the central bank raised interest rates for the first time since 2023.

Higher yields weighed broadly on equities, with bank stocks particularly hard hit as investors worried that rising borrowing costs would crimp lending activity. Goldman Sachs and Citigroup each fell nearly 2%, while Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and JPMorgan lost about 1%. Technology stocks also came under pressure amid concerns that higher rates could slow the artificial intelligence buildout. CrowdStrike shares dropped almost 4%, while Palo Alto Networks and Meta Platforms fell more than 3% and 2%, respectively.

Energy costs added to the pressure. International Brent crude futures rose above $101 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude hovered near $90. The spike was driven by renewed Houthi attacks in the Middle East and a tropical storm threatening the U.S. Gulf Coast, which prompted Chevron to evacuate nonessential personnel from offshore platforms. The rise in oil prices revived fears that inflation could remain stubbornly high, reinforcing the bond market's recent surge.

Investors are now focused on the Fed minutes, due at 2 p.m. ET, for clues on the central bank's future rate path. Traders are trying to determine whether September's rate hike was a one-off or a signal of further tightening. As of Tuesday, markets priced in roughly 20% odds of another hike at the Fed's October meeting. "With the level of rates where they are and the rise that we've seen, I think it's fair to characterize the fact that the margin for error has narrowed as it relates to earnings," said Mike Dickson, head of research and quantitative strategies at Horizon Investments, adding that earnings could "still carry the market higher."

On the earnings front, Constellation Brands fell 5% despite reporting better-than-expected results. The Corona and Modelo beer maker posted second-quarter net sales of $2.63 billion, above the $2.54 billion consensus, and adjusted earnings per share of $3.74, topping estimates of $3.55. The company cited a decline in off-premise sales at grocery and convenience stores, while on-premise sales at restaurants and bars grew. Constellation reaffirmed its full-year adjusted earnings forecast of $11.20 to $11.90 per share. Levi Strauss and Applied Digital are scheduled to report later.

stories.headline: AI Spending Fuels Market Optimism but Raises Inflation and Concentration Risks
body: The S&P 500 closed at an all-time high on Tuesday, rising 0.58 percent to top its previous peak from mid-August, as enthusiasm around artificial intelligence continued to drive a buying frenzy on Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite also hit a record, finishing up 0.45 percent. The S&P 500 is up 14 percent so far in 2026, and the Nasdaq has gained 18.78 percent, putting the market on track for a fourth consecutive year of double-digit returns. Tech stocks led the rally, with each of the "Magnificent Seven" except Meta closing higher; Amazon gained 1.95 percent, Microsoft rose 0.78 percent, and Nvidia added 0.14 percent.

The AI investment boom, however, is creating tensions that threaten global growth, according to IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. Speaking at a Wednesday event in Singapore, Georgieva described the global economy as being pulled in two directions: a "negative energy supply shock" from the war in the Gulf and a "positive demand shock" from AI investment. The combined effect, she said, is "highly uneven across the world." Global AI investment as a share of GDP is set to reach or exceed the amounts spent on building railroads, electricity grids, or telecommunications networks. AI hardware and related technology products already account for more than a tenth of world goods trade. The IMF estimates AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual world growth if done right, but the benefits are likely highly concentrated, bypassing economies less involved in the AI supply chain and "increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe."

Georgieva warned that the AI building boom is inflationary, alongside energy and food shocks, tariffs, and defense spending. Oil prices have stayed above $100 per barrel as the Middle East conflict drags on, and retail diesel prices have risen to record highs. That inflation pressure has flowed into bond markets, with yields in the U.S., Germany, and Japan surging to their highest levels in decades. Ballooning long-term private bond issuance by AI-related borrowers also competes with governments for capital. Global public debt is near its highest level since World War II and on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP, with advanced economies the "worst offenders." Higher interest rates have ended a 17-year period when rates stayed below growth rates, making it harder to reduce debt ratios without fiscal effort. "Fiscal space is crying out for replenishment," Georgieva said.

The World Bank, in its latest report on East Asia and the Pacific, raised its growth forecast for the region to 4.5% this year, citing AI-related exports, but warned that reliance on the AI boom leaves the region vulnerable to a potential global tech spending reversal. AI-related goods accounted for more than half of export growth in most of the region's economies and more than 70% in Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam shipped $1.4 trillion of AI-related goods in the 12 months through April. The World Bank highlighted that just two chipmakers — Samsung and SK Hynix — accounted for 43% of the value of South Korea's benchmark Kospi index as of end-April. AI-related capital expenditure has reached about 6% of U.S. GDP, similar to the 2000 peak in IT investment, and the current cycle "has risen faster than either previous cycle and is still gaining speed."

There are already signs the boom is cooling. HSBC Global Investment Research noted that prices for some key electronics are easing and that new order and inventory data point to a pullback in demand. Shipments from Asia have pulled back notably, including chip exports from Taiwan. While the slowdown may prove "a mere wobble" in a multiyear surge, a cooling AI hardware cycle would expose economic imbalances that have built up in Asia, according to HSBC. The Bank for International Settlements warned in June that the AI boom resembles the dot-com frenzy of the 1990s and other "manias." Of the $2.9 trillion in AI capex planned for 2025-2028, $800 billion is expected to come from private credit, where AI-related lending rose to 34% of activity in 2025 from an 18% average over the prior five years. Private credit portfolios have already experienced markdowns, outflows, and defaults this year, and the World Bank noted that private credit markets are "less visible, and have not been tested by a severe downturn."

Georgieva also pointed to a financial stability risk in the AI boom itself. Strong corporate earnings are driving share prices and wealth effects, she said, but "should earnings fall short, however, hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock." Citing Amara's Law — that people overestimate a new technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run — she said it is "somewhere in the transition between today's AI building boom and tomorrow's arrival of AI's benefits that we will traverse the period of maximum risk." She called for a "prudently hawkish bias" in monetary policy and said the first line of defense is regulation and supervision. The U.S. Federal Reserve raised rates last month, its first increase in more than three years, and signaled one more hike this year. A slowdown by 1 percentage point in U.S. growth would cut other emerging-market growth by an estimated 0.6 percentage point, with the hit to investment about twice as large, the World Bank said. "A slowdown concentrated in AI would be material for East Asia because of the region's prominence in the AI supply chain."

stories.headline: Inflation Expectations Jump to 3.9% as Dollar Rises Ahead of Fed Minutes
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Inflation expectations among U.S. consumers rose sharply in September, with the New York Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Expectations showing the median one-year outlook climbing to 3.9%, the highest level since May 2023. The reading, up 0.3 percentage point from August, comes as the Federal Reserve prepares to release minutes from its September policy meeting, when it raised interest rates for the first time since 2023. The U.S. dollar strengthened ahead of the release, with the dollar index rising 0.3% to 102.13, while gold prices fell 0.9% to $4,126.02 an ounce as a stronger dollar weighed on the precious metal.

The New York Fed survey also found that consumers expect household spending growth to hit 5.5%, also up 0.3 percentage point and the highest since May 2023. Longer-term expectations were more stable: the three-year outlook edged up 0.1 percentage point to 3.3%, while the five-year view held steady at 3%. Surging energy costs are a key driver of the inflation outlook; gasoline prices rose nearly 4% in August alone, and the survey showed consumers expect gas prices to rise 4.8% over the next year. Market-based measures also reflect inflation concerns, with the five-year breakeven rate near its 2025 high at 2.35%.

The Fed's September rate hike was its first since 2023, and projections released alongside the decision indicated further increases could occur before year-end as inflation remains above the central bank's 2% target. However, expectations for another hike at the Fed's October meeting have retreated following weaker-than-expected employment data and comments from policymakers signaling less urgency. According to CME FedWatch, the probability of a 25-basis-point hike in October stands at 21.6%, down from about 51% a week ago, while markets price in a 68.6% chance of a hike at the December meeting. Fed funds futures imply a rate of 5.58% in five years, compared with the current target range of 3.75%-4%.

Fed officials have offered mixed signals on the path ahead. New York Fed President John Williams said policymakers can afford to take their time evaluating where rates should be set, while Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said the central bank needs to raise its policy rate further to lower inflation, even if higher long-term yields are weighing on some parts of the economy. Several Fed officials, including Christopher Waller, Neel Kashkari, and Alberto Musalem, are scheduled to speak later Wednesday. The central bank is also due to release consumer credit data, expected to show a decrease to $15 billion in August from $18.06 billion in July.

The dollar's gains were supported by rising oil prices, with Brent futures climbing back above $100 a barrel on concerns over supply disruptions from a storm threatening U.S. oil-producing regions and attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on Aden International Airport. The euro fell 0.4% to $1.1216, giving back some of its gains from Tuesday when French bonds rallied after far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen raised her target for spending cuts to €140 billion ($158 billion). The yen weakened 0.13% to 158.31 per dollar, even after a dovish Bank of Japan board member signaled support for interest rate increases. Central bank demand for gold continued to provide support to the market, with the World Gold Council reporting that central banks added 39 tonnes of gold in August, bringing the year-to-date total to 170 tonnes.

stories.headline: U.S. Trade Deficit Widens to $105.6 Billion, Highest Since Pre-Tariff Era
body: The U.S. trade deficit widened sharply in August, hitting $105.6 billion amid an influx of goods tied to the artificial-intelligence build-out and the effects of import tariffs, the Commerce Department reported Tuesday. The figure marked a 13.7% jump from July and exceeded the Dow Jones consensus estimate of $102 billion.

Imports swelled 4.3% for the month, pushing the total imbalance to its steepest level since the all-time gap of March 2025, recorded just before President Donald Trump's 'liberation day' announcement of reciprocal tariffs against U.S. trading partners. Despite the monthly increase, the year-to-date deficit of $138.2 billion was down nearly 20% from the same period a year ago.

Oren Klachkin, financial economist at Nationwide, said in a note that 'rising prices overstate the moves, but nonetheless net trade is set to drag on Q3 GDP growth.' He added, 'We see this as a sign of strong domestic demand, not economic weakness.' Imports generally subtract from gross domestic product calculations, but if they reflect stronger demand and consumption, they can be offset elsewhere.

Following the report, Goldman Sachs cut its tracking estimate for third-quarter economic growth to 3.1%, down 0.3 percentage point from its prior estimate. The Atlanta Federal Reserve's GDPNow tracker lowered its estimate to 3.7%, down 0.1 percentage point from the last update.

stories.headline: MLB Division Series Day 5: Freeman sets lefty HR record, Padres win without Miller, Dodgers take 2-1 lead
body: Day 5 of the MLB Division Series delivered a full slate of action and developments across both leagues. The Los Angeles Dodgers took a 2-1 lead over the Atlanta Braves with a 3-1 victory in Game 3, moving within one win of eliminating the Braves and advancing to their third consecutive National League Championship Series. The San Diego Padres avoided elimination in the NLDS by beating the Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 at Petco Park, forcing a Game 4 on Wednesday. In the ALDS, the Tampa Bay Rays hold a commanding 2-0 series lead over the New York Yankees after a 5-2 win in Game 2, with Game 3 set for Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium.

Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman made postseason history Tuesday night, hitting a solo home run in the top of the fourth inning against Atlanta left-hander Chris Sale to give Los Angeles a 3-0 lead. The blast was the eighth lefty-on-lefty home run of Freeman's postseason career, establishing an MLB playoff record for left-handed hitters against left-handed pitchers, according to Elias Sports Bureau. Freeman, who spent his first 12 MLB seasons with the Braves before joining the Dodgers, batted .288 with 16 home runs during the regular season and is a former National League MVP and World Series MVP.

The Dodgers made a notable lineup change for Game 3, moving Shohei Ohtani from the No. 2 spot to fifth in the batting order. Manager Dave Roberts had opened the door to the adjustment, saying, "Going further than moving him from one to two, I'm open to it." Ohtani went 2-for-8 in the first two NLDS games and chased 42.9% of pitches outside the zone this postseason. Former MLB player Trevor Plouffe criticized the move to fifth as "disrespectful," arguing Ohtani should bat fourth instead. Ohtani was receptive to the change and had joked during a September slump about telling Roberts to hit him seventh. The Dodgers' starting lineup for Game 3 was Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Teoscar Hernandez, Will Smith, Shohei Ohtani, Miguel Rojas, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker and Kike Hernandez.

The Padres won Game 3 without All-Star closer Mason Miller, who was placed on the postseason paternity list Tuesday afternoon after his wife went into labor with the couple's first child. MLB approved the roster change, and the Padres replaced Miller with reliever Wandy Peralta. Under postseason paternity rules, Miller can miss a minimum of one day and a maximum of three; when he returns, he can replace Peralta without being forced to sit out another series. Miller had a career-high 38 saves this season with a 1.67 ERA. Peralta, a 35-year-old lefty, made 65 appearances this season and went 3-3 with a 3.61 ERA. Miller is eligible to return for Game 4 on Wednesday. The Padres had lost Games 1 and 2 by one run each, and Miller blew the save in Game 2 when Jackson Chourio hit a walk-off single that drove in two runs for a 4-3 Milwaukee victory.

In the ALDS, the Rays have taken a 2-0 series lead over the Yankees with a 1-0 win in Game 1 behind Drew Rasmussen and a 5-2 victory in Game 2 behind Freddy Peralta. Game 3 is scheduled for Wednesday at 8 p.m. ET at Yankee Stadium, with Tampa Bay expected to start right-hander Nick Martinez (15-6, 3.10 ERA) and New York expected to counter with left-hander Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA). The Yankees are a -164 favorite on the money line, with an over/under of 7 runs. SportsLine's computer model, which simulates every game 10,000 times, projects the over to hit 54% of the time and recommends betting over 7 combined runs.

Looking ahead, the Dodgers can eliminate the Braves with a win in Game 4 on Wednesday in Atlanta; if the Braves force a Game 5, it will be played Friday in Los Angeles. The Padres and Brewers continue their series with Game 4 on Wednesday in San Diego. The Yankees and Rays play Game 3 on Wednesday night, with the Rays seeking a sweep and the Yankees trying to avoid a 3-0 deficit.

stories.headline: Senior figures concerned Manchester City could play Champions League despite relegation
body: Senior figures within English football are concerned that Manchester City could play in the Champions League next season even if they are relegated from the Premier League for breaching financial regulations, BBC Sport has reported. The concern centers on the possibility that City win the Champions League this season, which would provide qualification as titleholders regardless of their status in the English domestic pyramid. BBC Sport has been told there is no automatic mechanism to remove City from a European competition they qualify for on sporting merit.

An independent commission found City guilty of all charges related to inflating sponsorship revenue by £830m using sham contracts, as well as hiding other expenses worth an additional £90m. Without this, the commission said, City would have failed profit and sustainability rules in all nine seasons between 2009-10 and 2017-18. City continue to strenuously deny any wrongdoing, calling the outcome a 'Premier League conspiracy,' and last week lodged an appeal against the verdict.

The immediate issue surrounds the Uefa licence every club needs to play in Europe. Licences are issued by the Football Association, though the process is delegated to the Premier League. They are based on current information and do not take into account sanctions or breaches related to historical offences. One source said the issue of City's licence 'had been raised' and that a solution 'would require the sort of joined up thinking that's been a bit lacking so far.' A source added that 'licences are awarded on the basis of current financial performance, so the grounds to refuse one are unclear.'

If the verdict is upheld by the appeal board, City could face severe sanctions including heavy points deductions, a large fine, transfer embargoes, or even immediate expulsion from the Premier League. The sanctioning hearing has not yet been scheduled. While a points deduction could rule City out of qualifying by league position, qualification could still be achieved through cup competitions. If City win the FA Cup or Carabao Cup, that would provide a place in the Europa League or Conference League respectively.

European football's governing body cannot take any action while the Premier League disciplinary process plays out, but it is understood potential scenarios are likely to be discussed by the Uefa administration and the Uefa club financial control body (CFCB). Uefa may open a disciplinary case to find a way to remove City's eligibility, but City's offences are historical. In 2020, City successfully overturned a two-year European ban from Uefa at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) because the offences were 'time-barred' under Uefa's rules. If City are not successful in their appeal and win the Champions League, the CFCB will have to find a disciplinary measure to remove the club, but there is concern City could again win against Uefa through Cas.

stories.headline: WHO questions Russia on second plague lab death amid outbreak fears
body: The World Health Organization has asked Russia for more information about the death of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia and reports of a second employee with unexplained pneumonia, as authorities monitor nearly 200 contacts and quarantine at least one hospital. Daria Shipilova, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East—a facility that studies plague, anthrax, tularemia, and other high-consequence pathogens—was hospitalized on Sept. 29 with severe pneumonia and died about two days later. Russian officials have described her illness as pneumonia of unknown etiology and said testing has not identified a pathogen linked to her work, though early news reports speculated she may have had pneumonic plague.

The WHO said Russia has reported no confirmed cases of plague in Irkutsk and no evidence of further infections among monitored contacts, but it has requested clarification on the cause of Shipilova’s pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health response, and whether a second employee also has pneumonia of undetermined cause. Public health officials have sent senior officials to the region, and testing of contacts has identified COVID-19 and rhinovirus in a small number of cases. The WHO assessed the public health risk to the general population as low based on current information.

Infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli, a former WHO medical officer, wrote in a STAT column that the situation deserves attention but not panic. She noted that plague—caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis—is a known disease with effective antibiotics and established protocols for diagnosis, contact monitoring, and treatment, unlike the novel SARS-CoV-2 virus. Person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague generally requires close exposure to respiratory droplets from an actively ill person, and asymptomatic transmission has not been documented. Kuppalli emphasized that an unexplained pneumonia does not mean a new pandemic pathogen has emerged.

The case has drawn scrutiny because of Russia’s history with biological weapons research. The Soviet Union operated a clandestine biological weapons program despite being a party to the Biological Weapons Convention, including work with Yersinia pestis. In 1979, an accidental release of aerosolized anthrax spores from a military facility in Sverdlovsk killed at least 66 people; Soviet authorities initially blamed contaminated meat, but a 1994 investigation in Science confirmed an airborne release. Kuppalli said this history provides a legitimate reason to demand transparency and independent verification, but stressed there is no evidence linking the current situation to a biological weapons program.

CBS News medical contributor Dr. Céline Gounder said the American public does not need to be worried. Kuppalli called for Russia to share specimens, testing results, and details about Shipilova’s work and any occupational exposure. She warned against filling information gaps with speculation, writing, 'The appropriate response is neither panic nor blind reassurance, but a clear demand for transparency and data.' The WHO continues to seek further information from Russian authorities.

stories.headline: 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics awarded to Francis Halzen for IceCube neutrino observatory in Antarctica
body: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded to Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin-Madison for building a neutrino observatory buried under the ice in Antarctica. The project, known as IceCube, was initially met with widespread skepticism. 'This project, everybody thought is a cute idea that won't work,' Halzen told the Nobel committee.

IceCube is located at the South Pole and consists of more than 5,000 sensors frozen into a cubic kilometer of ice, more than a mile beneath the surface. The detector is designed to capture neutrinos — tiny, ghostly particles from deep space that rarely interact with matter. When a neutrino does create a flash of light in the ice, the sensors pick it up. However, the signal is extremely difficult to isolate: for every one neutrino from space, there are about a trillion particles generated in Earth's atmosphere that create background noise. Physicist Naoko Kurahashi Neilson of Drexel University, who has worked on the project, compared the challenge to picking out a single note from a chaotic musical arrangement.

Despite the difficulty, IceCube has begun to identify the sources of some neutrinos. Erin O'Sullivan, IceCube spokesperson and a professor at Uppsala University in Sweden, said the first such detection came in 2017, when the observatory recorded a neutrino from the direction of a blazar — a supermassive black hole. Other neutrinos have since been traced to sources within the Milky Way. Kurahashi Neilson described the current state of the data as resembling the static on an old television set, where patterns are just beginning to emerge.

The project involves 450 researchers across 14 countries. O'Sullivan offered congratulations on behalf of the collaboration: 'I think I speak on behalf of the whole collaboration when we say, congratulations, Francis, on this great achievement.' Halzen's vision, once dismissed as a cute idea that would not work, has become a functioning observatory that is gradually opening a new window on the universe.

stories.headline: Dutch court halts Merck's new Keytruda formulation in Europe
body: A Dutch court has ruled that Merck infringed on a patent held by Halozyme Therapeutics related to a subcutaneous formulation of its blockbuster cancer drug Keytruda, ordering the company to stop manufacturing and marketing the medication in several European countries. The ruling applies to France, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland, and the Netherlands.

The decision is part of a widening patent infringement dispute between Merck and Halozyme over the best-selling cancer treatment. The court’s order does not affect the existing intravenous version of Keytruda, which remains available to patients.
Merck said in a statement that it “strongly” disagreed with the court’s decision.

stories.headline: US government and Google join Zuckerberg's Biohub in $1.8B AI biology push
stories.byline: Tech / AI desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The US government and Google are joining forces with Biohub, the nonprofit biomedical research organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, in a $1.8 billion initiative to build artificial intelligence datasets for biology. Google DeepMind, Meta, and the AI drug discovery startup Isomorphic Labs are jointly investing $300 million into Biohub, as part of the broader effort to create AI models that could allow researchers to 'ask, predict, and answer biological questions digitally,' according to a press release cited by Reuters.

The initiative aims to develop a 'virtual cell' — an accurate predictive model of biology that would let scientists carry out simulations digitally, potentially accelerating the discovery of new ways to prevent and manage diseases. The US Department of Energy will invest more than $500 million over the next five years, while the National Institutes of Health will contribute datasets, repositories, and knowledge bases stemming from previous federal investment totaling over $500 million.

Biohub was founded in 2016 with the goal of combating diseases through the creation of a virtual cell. Alex Rives, Biohub's head of science, said in the press release: 'An accurate predictive model of biology could dramatically accelerate scientific discovery by enabling scientists to perform experiments digitally. The creation of a virtual cell is one of the most important challenges for the next era of science. It will require coordinated data generation efforts at a national and international scale, which is why these partners are coming together.'

The collaboration brings together private companies, a nonprofit research organization, and major US government agencies to tackle what they describe as a critical scientific challenge. The combined $1.8 billion in funding and data contributions is intended to generate the large-scale datasets needed to train AI systems capable of modeling biology with enough accuracy to replace some physical experiments with digital ones.

stories.headline: OpenAI Releases 722 Mathematical Manuscripts, DeepMind Publishes Aletheia Agent Research, Fueling Debate on AI Proof Verification
body: OpenAI released 722 mathematical manuscripts grouped into 372 result families on October 6, alongside selected formal proof artifacts and ten abridged reasoning summaries, according to the company's announcement. The release includes an average compute equivalent of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking per result and identifies the underlying model as unreleased. Google DeepMind separately published research on Aletheia, an AI agent that generates, critiques and revises mathematical arguments, along with reports on its performance in research studies. Neither release provides a matched experimental comparison that establishes which lab is superior at mathematical research, according to an analysis by Kingy AI.

OpenAI's formalization manifest describes its scope as "Partial progress" and its review status as unchecked, according to the release's README and formalization manifest. The company provides Comparator, a tool that under documented trust assumptions can establish that a selected solution proves a challenge's statement using only permitted axioms and is accepted by the Lean kernel. However, the formalization metadata does not supply an independent receipt showing that the entire collection passed verification. For example, Family 017's documentation selects the claim that π's irrationality exponent is exactly two but explicitly excludes the paper's Flint–Hills series convergence consequence from that selected statement.

DeepMind's Aletheia system uses a natural-language verifier inside the agent, followed by human assessment in research studies, according to the Aletheia report. An Erdős case study from December 2025 shows Aletheia attempted 700 problems and returned 212 potentially correct responses; human assessment classified 200 candidates definitively, of which 137 were fundamentally flawed, 63 were technically correct, and only 13 addressed the intended problem meaningfully—those 13 included results already present in the literature. A later FirstProof study reports six of ten problems solved under majority expert assessment, with "correct" meaning publishable after minor revisions; Problem 8 received five positive assessments from seven experts, and each configuration had at least one false positive.

OpenAI identifies two procedure exceptions—zeta zero-free-region work and Hodge work for CM abelian varieties—and discloses human editing for readability of the alternate zeta write-up reaching the region Re(s) > 11/12. The README does not provide an equivalent interaction record for every manuscript, limiting conclusions about human involvement across the collection. DeepMind's eigenweights paper by Tony Feng includes an AI-usage declaration attributing the core mathematical content to Aletheia, with Feng describing his contribution as rewriting the output into paper form and adding the introduction. Other DeepMind projects involve substantive human mathematical contributions, and the company's framework distinguishes autonomy from mathematical significance.

The releases support inspection more directly than independent reproduction of discovery, according to Kingy AI's assessment. OpenAI's Lean README recommends compiling small portions and documents a Linux memory-mapping issue that can affect whole-library builds. DeepMind's repository links prompts and responses for individual projects, including FirstProof, and notes that two included outputs came from systems other than Aletheia. Neither release provides a complete, equivalent public environment for rerunning either research pipeline. A fair cost comparison between the two systems would require the same problems, a common acceptance standard, attempt limits, tool access, measured resource use, and inclusion of failed attempts, formalization costs, and human review—none of which the current disclosures supply.

The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence explicitly states its advisory role does not endorse OpenAI's process or judge the impact of the results, according to its responsible-release recommendations. The group's recommendations ask for model identification and further disclosure. OpenAI says it is working toward releasing the model. DeepMind's earlier formal results, including the 2024 IMO evaluation where AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 jointly solved four of six problems for a silver-medal-standard score, involved humans translating problems into formal language and solutions taking up to three days. Those contest problems differ from research lemmas and proposed resolutions of long-standing conjectures, and their scores should retain those labels, according to the analysis.
